comparison: Use coordinate means and centered coordinate covariances for the two populations, requiring the same finite matrix Sigma to be positive definite. The two hypotheses are equality and inequality of the mean vectors, respectively, not equality of the full laws. Second-moment finiteness is part of the source model; the total real covariance integral alone does not certify it. PosDef supplies Hermitian symmetry and strict positivity on nonzero vectors, with finite-dimensional coordinates reconciling its finitely supported-vector formulation. Do not replace the common covariance by two unequal matrices, assume Gaussian populations, or infer positive definiteness of each empirical covariance from positive definiteness of Sigma.
gap: Covariance and positive-definiteness predicates express the population model; its sampling assumptions and mean-testing hypotheses must be supplied explicitly.
searches: Inspect covariance and Matrix.PosDef against the common-covariance two-population model
Centered scalar covariances can be assembled coordinatewise and PosDef supplies strict matrix positivity; neither declares a two-sample statistical testing model.

comparison: Apply family independence and equality of pushforward laws to the standardized scalar coordinates w_j, impose their zero means, unit second moments and finite fourth moment kappa, then transform by the positive square root of the common positive-definite Sigma and add the appropriate population mean. Fourth-moment integrability can be expressed by MemLp at exponent four; the numerical moment equalities remain separate. Independence and identical distribution concern the input coordinates, not the coordinates after a general mixing square root. Retain the source's random-sample setup separately and do not promote the representation to normality, independence of the two means, or equality of population means under the alternative.
gap: Independence, identical laws, moment integrability and matrix powers provide the model's components, with its moment equalities and affine representation still to be specified.

comparison: Define f_u pointwise by max(f(t),u), and take the supremum of the scalar heights u-M(f) whose L2 distance from f on [0,1] is at most epsilon. The domain and Lebesgue measure must be retained: a supremum norm or a norm on the whole real line changes the quantity. The extended L2 norm can be compared directly with the finite budget, avoiding conversion of an infinite norm to a real zero. For the source's finite convex function with an attained minimum, u=M(f) gives an admissible zero height, and boundedness on the unit interval bounds the admissible heights above; these facts justify a real conditional supremum. The supremum definition alone need not claim an attained optimizer or uniqueness of the clipping level. No white-noise distribution is involved in this deterministic construction.
gap: Pointwise maximum, L2 seminorm and supremum operations express the clipping-height definition once its finite-budget domain conditions are established.

comparison: For a function whose domain is the subtype O, HasCompactSupport means its nonzero support has compact closure in O, preserving compact support within the open domain rather than merely compact ambient closure touching its boundary. Combine this with the appropriate smoothness or source function-space membership. The source's C(overline O) explicitly means uniformly continuous functions on O; replacing it by arbitrary ContinuousOn O would weaken that convention. H_c^k consists of compactly supported members, whereas H_0^k is the completion of smooth compactly supported functions in the H^k norm. They are not interchangeable, and the continuous dual used in Theorem 11 retains the inherited H1 norm on H_c^1. The inspected whole-space Fourier/Bessel-potential Sobolev predicate does not directly establish these domain spaces or identify their closures.
gap: Compact support and smoothness are available, while the source's domain Sobolev spaces, inherited dual norm and completion require additional definitions and identifications.
searches: Inspect Support.lean 207-217 and ContDiffOn; search Sobolev in Analysis and MeasureTheory and inspect Distribution/Sobolev.lean 149-155
HasCompactSupport uses the domain topology; the located Sobolev predicate is for tempered distributions via Bessel potentials, not these compact-support subspaces and their domain-norm completions.

comparison: Define two functions on the three specified kernel choices: order d equals 5, 6, 4 and multiplier Delta equals 40, 60, 2/3 for D, R, tau-star respectively. These are alternatives selected by the actual kernel, not simultaneous constraints on one object or formulas for arbitrary kernels. The multiplier should take real or rational values so that 2/3 is not natural-number division. A three-constructor kernel tag or nested piecewise function represents the table exactly; it does not prove that these multipliers normalize variances or establish the normal limit. Those statistical identities belong to separate statements.
